scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance is associated with the Malacca Sultanate, specifically the era of Sultan Mahmud Shah.
When the Sultan retreated to Sungai Muar, the dance was performed in the palace context for him and state dignitaries.
It originated as a court dance before becoming a folk tradition in Johor.
on_screen: Map: Malaysia · Southeast Asia
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a dance of royal homage, it now symbolizes happiness and well-being.
It is a staple of Malay weddings in Johor, used to honor the couple and invoke a sense of prosperity through the symbolism of light.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers perform with 'Golden Flowers' and lit candles.
It is performed by an odd number of dancers (usually 5–8) or in male-female pairs.
The movements incorporate 'worship duli' (homage) and gestures of humility.
Watch for Worship Duli.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The community of Kampung Baru Lenga, Batu 28, in the Muar District of Johor is noted as the primary practitioners and keepers of this specific dance tradition.
While popular across Johor, the most famous variant is localized to the Muar District, specifically Kampung Baru Lenga.
Traces back to the 16th-century Malacca Sultanate court and has been preserved as a folk dance in the Johor region.
